## UNESCO and Theory: A Recognition That Does Not Translate into Practice

The dossier sent to Paris carried the backing of autonomous communities, provincial councils, bishoprics, and dozens of local associations. The candidacy for manual bell ringing was built on the idea that Spain preserves one of the richest and most diverse sonic heritages on the continent, with dialectal variants that change from valley to valley and from bell tower to bell tower. UNESCO accepted the arguments and in 2022 inscribed the practice on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The announcement was celebrated in many municipalities as a symbolic victory, an international boost that would shield the bell ringing from oblivion.

In Almuñécar, the news was met with a mixture of pride and skepticism. The veteran bell ringers, those who still climb the towers of the Encarnación or the parish of San Miguel, knew that the recognition did not come with any specific obligations for the town councils. UNESCO does not impose binding safeguarding plans nor transfer direct funds to municipalities. Its seal is a moral distinction, a reminder that the international community considers a practice valuable, but day-to-day management still depends on local political will and municipal budgets.

Three years after the inscription, the local brotherhoods denounce that the recognition has not translated into a single tangible measure. There is no municipal school for bell ringers, no training program for young people, and no budget allocation dedicated to the conservation of the bell sets. The historical bronzes of Almuñécar, some cast in the 18th century, remain exposed to the elements, mounted on wooden headstocks that are cracking and fitted with clappers that strike with more force than the structures can withstand. The UNESCO declaration has not changed a single bolt of that reality.

The case of Almuñécar is not an exception in the Andalusian landscape. Inscription on the UNESCO representative list does not automatically generate state or regional funding lines for municipalities that preserve traditional ringing. The aid that does exist is usually tied to architectural restoration projects, not to the transmission of intangible knowledge. A bell tower may receive funds to repair cracks or consolidate walls, but hardly to pay a master bell ringer to teach the tolls for the dead, for festivities, or for alarms to a new generation.

The brotherhoods of Almuñécar have raised on more than one occasion the need to create a bell ringing school that operates on a stable basis. The proposal does not require major investments: it would suffice to set up a space in some parish facility, establish a practice schedule, and rely on the availability of the veteran bell ringers who still hold the complete repertoire. However, the initiative has found no echo in the City Council, which has not included manual bell ringing in its heritage programs or its cultural activities offerings. UNESCO recognition is mentioned in official speeches, but it does not appear in the budgets.

The protection of historical bell sets is another pending task. In Almuñécar, there are bronzes over two centuries old, pieces that have survived wars, earthquakes, and liturgical reforms. Some bear inscriptions with the founder's name, the date of casting, and the dedication to which they were consecrated. These items are not cataloged as movable assets of cultural interest, nor do they have a preventive conservation plan regulating their handling. UNESCO recognizes the value of the ringing, but does not require the protection of the instruments that make it possible.

The paradox is evident to those who know the ground. The international community declares that manual bell ringing is a heritage of humanity, while in Almuñécar the bell ringers who practice it receive no financial compensation or administrative recognition whatsoever. They climb the towers out of devotion, out of habit, or out of a sense of responsibility that is not stipulated in any contract. If one of them stops showing up, the ringing is lost, and no one has a legal obligation to replace them. UNESCO has put the spotlight on the practice, but the spotlight does not warm the bell towers.

Intangible heritage experts insist that effective safeguarding requires measures for transmission, documentation, and support for the bearer communities. Without those three pillars, inscription on the UNESCO list becomes an empty gesture, a plaque hung on the wall while the knowledge silently fades away. In Almuñécar, the documentation of local ringing is fragmentary and scattered: some are recorded on cassette tapes kept in private homes, others exist only in the memory of the oldest bell ringers. There is no municipal sound archive capturing the complete repertoire, nor an inventory of the ringing practiced in each parish.

The distance between theory and practice is measured in meters, not kilometers. One only needs to climb the tower of the Encarnación and observe the condition of the clappers, the frayed ropes, and the headstocks that creak with every toll. UNESCO has said that this sound is valuable to all of humanity. The brotherhoods of Almuñécar hope that someone, in some office at the City Council or the Junta de Andalucía, will translate that declaration into a budget allocation, a training program, or a simple maintenance order. Until now, administrative silence contrasts with the noise of the bells that still endure.
